Dear INLA-helpers

i was wondering if INLA can handle more than one spatial field, for example two fields with different meshes (or two spde-models):
y = A1*z1 + A2*z2 + e
z1 ~ N(0,Q1)
z2 ~ N(0,Q2)
e ~ N(0,sigma*I)

It would be great if you could help look at the following test codes for the above model..
Thank you very much for your help!

Ran.

## Test codes:

n = 100
loc1 = matrix(runif(n*2),n,2)

mesh1 =
  inla.mesh.create.helper(points=loc1,
                          cutoff=0.1,
                          max.edge=c(0.2,1),
                          min.angle=c(30,30),
                          offset=c(0.1,0.3))

loc2 = matrix(runif(n*2),n,2)

mesh2 =
  inla.mesh.create.helper(points=loc2,
                          cutoff=0.1,
                          max.edge=c(10,100),
                          min.angle=c(26,21),
                          offset=c(1,10))

#### Calculate mapping between the mesh nodes and the observation locations:
#  A: mapping stations to mesh nodes
A1 = inla.spde.make.A(mesh1, loc=loc1)
A2 = inla.spde.make.A(mesh2, loc=loc2)

#### Create SPDE objects
spde1 = inla.spde2.matern(mesh1, alpha=2)
summary(spde1)

spde2  = inla.spde2.matern(mesh2, alpha=2)
summary(spde2)

#### Simulate "the true" fields
true.kappa = sqrt(8)/0.3 ## Spatial range 0.3
true.tau   = 1/sqrt(4*pi*true.kappa^2) ## Variance = 1
true.field1 = inla.spde.sample(spde1, theta=log(c(true.tau, true.kappa)))
true.field2 = inla.spde.sample(spde2, theta=log(c(true.tau, true.kappa)))

#### Writing INLA formulas and Calculating results

data.stack = inla.stack(data=list(y=y),
                        A = list(A1,A2),
                        effects=list(list(field1=1:mesh1$n),
                                         list(field2=1:mesh2$n)))

data  = list(y=y, field1 = 1:mesh1$n, field2 = 1:mesh2$n)
formula = y ~ -1 + f(field1, model = spde1) + f(field2, model = spde2)

# This gives an error back:
result =
  inla(formula,
       data = inla.stack.data(data.stack, spde1=spde1, spde2 = spde2),
       family = "normal",
       control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(data.stack)), verbose=TRUE)

messages.subject: Re: spde for R3 mesh
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

the documentation for this advanced stuff is very much not written yet...
Some notes below:

On Tuesday, 11 September 2012 11:53:27 UTC+1, Ran wrote:
> I calculated the \tilde{C}, G and B matrices for a tetrahedral mesh in R3 and would like to try INLA for my model.
> When I create a spde object with boundary segments, I suppose that spde$internal$c0 is the \tilde{C} matrix, spde$internal$g1 is the B matrix and spde$internal$g2 is the G matrix due to its numbers of nonzeros in the sparse matrices, am I right?

No, not quite.  g1 is G and g2 is G*inv(C)*G, and we don't use B in the inla models at all, since we've only implemented Neumann boundary conditions.  Replacing G with G-B as in the theory unfortunately leads to strange models, so avoid that for now. I manipulated some of the parameters of the spde object like the following example:

> spde$internal$c0 = Ct
> spde$internal$g1 = B
> spde$internal$g2 = G
> spde$f$n = dim(Ct)[1]

Unfortunately, that won't work, due to the way these objects interact with the inla program.

> Since I just blindly manipulate some inputs, I suppose, INLA would not work (certainly your codes are not simple). I am just wondering if there is a quick solution for using INLA with a R3 mesh (like changing some input parameters for S2 spde objects to make a R3 spde object) or you have to implement the whole thing..

Yes, fortunately there is an alternative method for constructing more generic spde models that you can use instead, and which should be much easier to deal with, and which doesn't need to know anything about your mesh:
inla.spde2.generic

This functions constructs inla model objects with a specific precision matrix structure, where one can specify the different building blocks.  This is used by the inla.spde2.matern function to create Matern models on ordinary triangulation meshes, and what you need is a corresponding wrapper function for your 3D meshes.

When you have your computed C and G matrices, the following code should produce an SPDE model with alpha=2, i.e.
(kappa^2 - Laplacian ) (tau x(s)) = W(s)

spde = inla.spde2.generic(
 M0 = C,
 M1 = G,
 M2 = G %*% inla.qsolve(C, G),
 B0 = cbind(0, 1, 0), ## Make theta1 control log(tau)
 B1 = cbind(0, 0, 2), ## Make theta2 control log(kappa)
 B2 = cbind(1, 0, 0), transform="identity"), ## Unused part of the generic model; don't change
 theta.mu <http://theta.mu> = c(0, 0), theta.Q = diag(2) )

Then you'll likely need some more details to use this in an inla model, but hopefully this can get you started.
For example, you can check if the models seems sensible by simulating a sample:

sample = inla.spde.sample(spde, theta=log(c(some.tau, some.kappa)))

The interpretation of kappa should in your 3D case roughly be sqrt(8*0.5) / spatial.range

/Finn

messages.subject_clean: Using SPDE from Lindgren et al. (2011)
messages.body_plain:
Answers below; some interleaved with your code, some at the end.

On Thursday, 13 September 2012 14:23:44 UTC+1, Jon  wrote:

> ## The variable locs.full contains the spatial locations we would like to predict #at. It is an m by 2 vector #of coordinates.
>
> # The variable obs contains the spatial locations we have observed data at. It is #an n by 2 vector of #coordinates.

Since elsewhere it's clear that you want to have a model on a sphere, the above indicates to me that you have supplied your coordinates as (longitude, latitude), or some other planar mapping of the sphere.
Proper models on a globe require correct topology and distance metric (very obvious close to the poles, not so obvious/required if all data are near the equator). For this reason, the meshing code in inla can build meshes of the sphere itself, when the user supplies the cartesian 3D-coordinates of the locations.  To do this, convert your (lon,lat) points to (x,y,z):

First, convert the lon,lat to radians (multiply by 180/pi), and then construct the cartesian coordinates through

loc = cbind(cos(lat)*cos(lon), cos(lat)*sin(lon), sin(lat))

Feeding this M-by-3 matrix into inla.mesh.create produces a meshed version of a unit radius sphere.

The output verctor from inla() can then be projected back onto a regular lon-lat-lattice, if needed for plotting purposes, say, with the inla.mesh.project and inla.mesh.projector functions.

> #I’ve left out items (1), (2) and (3) for two reasons: it is not clear to me that this #produces predictions similar to the example in > Section 4 of the jrssb,  and #SPDE becomes slow as one includes more paramers.

Those lines of code construct a non-stationary field model, where the parameters of the spde are allowed to vary slowly with latitude.

spde = inla.spde.create(mesh = mesh, model = "matern", param=list(alpha=2))

This produces a stationary field model.

> #When looking at the Cameletti et al. paper it appears that this gives a modeling approach similar to Sections 1 and 2 of the jrssb paper (i.e., precisions are based on Main Result 2 in Section 2.3). Is that #correct?

Yes.

> # The result object appears to be giving approximate posterior distributions #based on INLA. However, I’m not sure what the prior specifications are, and I #need to report exactly what they are. Is there an equation line in the #references, or some default option that I can report?

The prior for the spde model can be seen in
  spde$f$hyper.default
and by default the priors are Gaussian.  In particular for the newer spde models produced by inla.spde2.matern, the priors are chosen heuristically to match the spatial scale of the mesh domain, but for inla.spde.create the user can set them manually.
In both cases, the user can override the defaults by supplying a "hyper" parameter to the f()-function in the formula.

For all other parts of inla models, the default priors are listed in the output from inla.models(), e.g.
 inla.models()$latent$rw2$hyper

as well as in the documentation on http://www.r-inla.org/models

> (a)    (a) Does the specification of the Delaunay triangulation look standard or correct? If not or if you don't have enough information, what resources are available so I use a standard choice for the Delaunay triangulation.

See my comments above.  The specific settings needed for inla.mesh.create are problem-dependent, and so requires more specific information for me to tell.  I am working on a tutorial text that will include some general guidelines for this.

> (b)   (b) How does one change the code so that the Delaunay triangulation does not extend outside the borders of the globe? Does that go against the methodology if I choose not to extend outside the borders of the globe?

See above; "outside the globe" is not an issue when the mesh is build on the actual globe surface!

> (c)    (c) Do items (1), (2), and (3) produce predictions similar to Section 4 of the jrssb paper? If not or if you don't have enough information, what resources are available so I can produce similar predictions.

Again, this is problem dependent.  The question has to begin with what kind of *model* is wanted/needed.

> (d)   (d) How many parameters are reasonable to include for spatial prediction using this SPDE approach?

The number of parameters influences the speed and memory requirements for parameter estimation, which for spatial models can be substantial for non-stationary models.  The largest models I've run used around 18 parameters and 20 times 16000 mesh nodes, but I wouldn't recommend you to try that unless you really need it, and understand the underlying non-stationary models.
There are several general options in inla to simplify the full Bayesian inference, allowing more complex models to run in shorter time, such as Empirical Bayes, and using Gaussian approximations without skewness corrections, and so on.

> (e)   (e) Will the uncommented spde object provide predictions similar to Sections 1 and 2 of the jrssb paper?

That depends on how you use it in your model, i.e. it is problem-dependent.

> (f)     (f) Exactly what priors are being used?

>  See above.

/Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] inla.mesh.project for ID
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The ID column is nothing but an index, and you cannot use it for your intended purpose.

The Cameletti paper code is written to perform prediction onto a dense grid in situations where this is too much for inla to handle memory-wise. If your problem is small enough or your computer big enough to let inla handle the full prediction, I recommend replacing the prediction "stack" in the Cameletti code by your intended full prediction grid&covariates in your second in.a call. (We have written some preliminary code to automate this, but it is not yet ready for public us.)  It would also be possible to use "lincomb", but that option has drawbacks for large sparse linear combinations for implementation design reasons.  Which method is more efficient is problem dependent.

Finn
